title: Work close
hookLine: sixty days on work, and the last move: finish, look, rest

cards: A carpenter sets down the plane, runs a palm along the tabletop, and steps back. Not to start the next job. Just to look.
That small pause is where this whole stretch on work ends. It began with a garden that needed tending.
Since then: a craftsman filled with spirit, a tentmaker, a farmer Guru, a woodworker who fasted before he carved, a Chan master who wouldn't eat on a day he didn't work.
This week alone: a harvest, a written answer to what your work really is, service, attention, and five different answers. Today, the last move. Finish.

teach.b: First, finishing. Back on day eight hundred eighty-six, Rabbi Tarfon said it isn't yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop. That's true of the big work: justice, a family, a life.
But inside it are small things that can be finished. A drawer. A letter.
Finishing one is its own kind of practice. Second, looking. Again and again in the creation story, Genesis pauses to look.

teach.h: AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.
teach.b: At the end of the sixth day, the King James says: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." The work isn't over until someone looks at it. Not to find the flaw.

teach.h: HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.
teach.b: The next verses don't start a new project: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made."
In that story, rest isn't what's left when the work runs out. It's part of the shape. Fourth, the whole block in one line.
The traditions gave very different answers about what work is. But across the texts on this path, one rhythm kept showing up: the Benedictine hours, the Sabbath, Friday prayers, the observance days.
Work well, then rest. Ecclesiastes says there's a season for everything, "and a time to every purpose under the heaven."
Work had its season here. Tomorrow a new question begins.

how: Several traditions pair work with set times of rest: the Jewish Sabbath, Christian Sunday rest, Friday congregational prayer in Islam, monastic hours of prayer, and Buddhist observance days.

o: a set-apart day of rest that gives work its shape
any long holiday spent away from home and work
a day for finishing the jobs left over from the week

games.q: closing the work — tap the pairs.
p: not yours to finish, nor free to stop
he rested on the seventh day

s: in Genesis, God starts a new project right after the sixth day
"he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made."
in Genesis, God looks at what was made and calls it very good
"And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good."
Rabbi Tarfon said you must finish all the work yourself
he said it isn't yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop.

games.q: the work is done. you're God in Genesis, at the end of the sixth day. what comes next?
o: look at it, call it good, then rest.
games.why: Genesis has God look and see that it was very good, then rest on the seventh day. the looking and the rest are part of the work's shape.

practice: Picture one small thing you could finish, one email, one shelf, one mended button, and see yourself doing it with care to the last step.

Then see yourself stepping back, like the carpenter, just looking, no checking for mistakes, and let your hands rest in your lap. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the work of these weeks.

wordCard.voice: Sabbath. The end of sixty days on work: finish something, look at it, and rest. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: work well, then rest. The stopping is part of the shape. See you tomorrow.
